source_refs.note: Book p. 49-50: 4.2.2 Subtraction of Matrices and Example 1 ((A + B)^t = A^t + B^t), whose solution continues on p. 50. Teaching notes, the extra steps of the example, Key points and Common mistake are ours.

blocks.text: If \(A = [a_{ij}]\) and \(B = [b_{ij}]\) are matrices of order \(m \times n\), then we define the subtraction of \(B\) from \(A\) as
Thus, the matrix \(A - B\) is formed by subtracting each entry of \(B\) from the corresponding entry of \(A\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: \(-B\) is the matrix whose entries are the negatives of the entries of \(B\) (it is \((-1)B\), see 4.2.3). So subtraction is just addition of \(-B\), and it has the same condition: \(A\) and \(B\) must have the same order. Order matters in subtraction: \(B - A = -(A - B)\), so in general \(A - B \ne B - A\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our example (not from the book):
\[\begin{bmatrix}5 & 3 \\ 2 & 7\end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix} 5-1 & 3-4 \\ 2-(-2) & 7-0 \end{bmatrix}\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix}4 & -1 \\ 4 & 7\end{bmatrix}\]
Note \(2 - (-2) = 4\): subtracting a negative entry adds.
The book's Example 1, printed right after this definition, practises addition and transposes together.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.problem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & -1 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\), then show that \((A + B)^{t} = A^{t} + B^{t}\).
steps:
Given: \(A\) and \(B\), both of order \(3 \times 4\).
To prove: \((A + B)^{t} = A^{t} + B^{t}\).
Method: work out each side separately. Left side: add first, then transpose. Right side: transpose each matrix, then add. If the two results are equal matrices, the statement is shown.

Step 1: Find \(A + B\)
\[A + B = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\]
\[+ \begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & -1 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]
Row 1: \(1+2,\ 0+(-1),\ -1+3,\ 2+1\)
Row 2: \(3+1,\ 1+3,\ 2+(-1),\ 5+4\)
Row 3: \(0+3,\ -2+1,\ 1+2,\ 6+(-1)\)
\[A + B = \begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 4 & 1 & 9 \\ 3 & -1 & 3 & 5\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: \(A\) and \(B\) have the same order \(3 \times 4\), so they are conformable for addition; we add the entries in the same positions.

Step 2: Transpose the sum
\[(A + B)^{t} = \begin{bmatrix}3 & 4 & 3 \\ -1 & 4 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9 & 5\end{bmatrix} \quad \text{(i)}\]
Why: the 1st row \(3, -1, 2, 3\) of \(A + B\) becomes the 1st column, the 2nd row the 2nd column, and the 3rd row the 3rd column. The order changes from \(3 \times 4\) to \(4 \times 3\).

Step 3: Transpose \(A\) and \(B\)
\[A^{t} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 5 & 6\end{bmatrix}\]
\[B^{t} = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 3 \\ -1 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 & -1\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: the right side needs the transposes first; rows of each matrix become its columns.

Step 4: Add the transposes
Row 1: \(1+2,\ 3+1,\ 0+3\)
Row 2: \(0+(-1),\ 1+3,\ -2+1\)
Row 3: \(-1+3,\ 2+(-1),\ 1+2\)
Row 4: \(2+1,\ 5+4,\ 6+(-1)\)
\[A^{t} + B^{t} = \begin{bmatrix}3 & 4 & 3 \\ -1 & 4 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9 & 5\end{bmatrix} \quad \text{(ii)}\]
Why: \(A^{t}\) and \(B^{t}\) are both \(4 \times 3\), so they can be added entry by entry.

Step 5: Compare (i) and (ii)
The two matrices have the same order \(4 \times 3\) and every pair of corresponding entries is equal, so
\[(A + B)^{t} = A^{t} + B^{t}\]
Why: by the definition of equal matrices (4.1).

Check: one entry by hand. Row 2, column 3 of \((A + B)^{t}\) is the entry in row 3, column 2 of \(A + B\), that is \(-2 + 1 = -1\). In \(A^{t} + B^{t}\) the same place holds \(-2 + 1 = -1\). They agree.
blocks.answer: From (i) and (ii), \((A + B)^{t} = A^{t} + B^{t}\). Hence shown.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Example 1 shows for these particular matrices a rule that is true for all matrices of the same order: the transpose of a sum is the sum of the transposes. The reason: the entry in row \(i\), column \(j\) of \((A + B)^{t}\) is \(a_{ji} + b_{ji}\), and that is exactly the entry in the same place of \(A^{t} + B^{t}\). The same is true for a difference: \((A - B)^{t} = A^{t} - B^{t}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(A - B = A + (-B) = [a_{ij} - b_{ij}]\); it needs \(A\) and \(B\) of the same order.
2. Subtract entry by entry, always \(A\)'s entry minus \(B\)'s entry.
3. \(A - B \ne B - A\) in general; \(B - A = -(A - B)\).
4. \((A + B)^{t} = A^{t} + B^{t}\) (Example 1).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Subtracting in the wrong order (\(b_{ij} - a_{ij}\)), which changes every sign.
2. Sign slips with negative entries: \(2 - (-2) = 4\), not 0.
3. In Example 1, writing a row of \(A + B\) as a row of \((A + B)^{t}\) instead of as a column.
